channel.title: Notes on Miro's World
channel.description: Recent content in Notes on Miro's World

item.description:
Whatever I sit down to do with an AI coding assistant, the session ends the same way: the token budget is gone. It does not seem to matter what the task was. Fix one small bug, plan a migration, write a three-paragraph note like this one - by the end I am watching the context meter instead of the work.

For a while I read that as bad estimation on my part. I think it is something duller. The work is not what costs; the situating is. Before anything useful happens, the assistant has to be told where it is: which repo, which conventions, what was decided last week and why, which of my rules are real rules. That bill is roughly the same whether the edit that follows is one line or two hundred. So a trivial task and a serious one cost about the same to start, and only the serious one feels worth it afterwards.

My company, Klassify s.r.o., finally has a web page: klassify.com. Until now the domain carried only my email, and anyone who looked it up from an invoice or a contract found nothing at all.

It is a single static page, no framework: who Klassify is, what kind of engagements I take, the certifications, and where to find more. The “more” is this blog, so the landing page points here, and this note points back.

Most of my note-taking and thinking happens in Obsidian, so natural extension of this tool was to allow a pipeline that allows me to publish a thought or a quick note directly from Obsidian Vault into the this blog.

Every note starts its life as obsidian note, and through dedicated set of tags and custom attribute for publishing, it finds its way to the repository holding the source of this blog. Then another pipeline: the one that pre-compiles static website and publishes to GitHub takes over and makes the note visible.
This blog now has a notes stream — short things that don’t warrant a full post. It has its own RSS feed. This is the first one, mostly to prove the machinery works.
